chronology.label: Kennedy challenges nation to Moon landing
chronology.detail: President John F. Kennedy addressed the United States Congress on 'Urgent National Needs' and declared commitment to achieving the goal of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely before the end of the decade.

chronology.label: Kennedy's Rice University speech
chronology.detail: Kennedy delivered a speech before a crowd of about 40,000 people in the Rice University football stadium in Houston, Texas, declaring 'We choose to go to the Moon in this decade.'

chronology.label: Kennedy proposes joint Moon mission to Khrushchev
chronology.detail: Kennedy met with Nikita Khrushchev, the Premier of the Soviet Union, and proposed making the Moon landing a joint project, but Khrushchev declined the offer.

chronology.label: Kennedy proposes joint Moon mission to UN
chronology.detail: Kennedy proposed a joint expedition to the Moon in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly.

chronology.label: Apollo 1 fire
chronology.detail: Project Apollo was abruptly halted by the Apollo 1 fire in which astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger B. Chaffee died.

chronology.label: Sputnik 1 launch
chronology.detail: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, surprising the world and fueling fears about Soviet technological and military capabilities.

chronology.label: Yuri Gagarin first in space
chronology.detail: Cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space and the first to orbit the Earth.

chronology.label: Alan Shepard first American in space
chronology.detail: Alan Shepard became the first American in space; his 15-minute flight was suborbital, not a full orbit.

chronology.label: LM-5 Eagle ascent stage arrives at Kennedy
chronology.detail: The ascent stage of LM-5 Eagle arrived at the Kennedy Space Center on January 8, 1969.

chronology.label: LM-5 Eagle descent stage arrives
chronology.detail: The descent stage of LM-5 Eagle arrived four days after the ascent stage at the Kennedy Space Center.

chronology.label: CSM-107 Columbia arrives
chronology.detail: The Command and Service Module CSM-107 Columbia arrived at Kennedy Space Center.

chronology.label: CSM and LM mated
chronology.detail: The CSM was mated to the LM.

chronology.label: Spacecraft moved to VAB
chronology.detail: The mated spacecraft moved from the Operations and Checkout Building to the Vehicle Assembly Building.

chronology.label: Saturn V moved to launch pad
chronology.detail: At 12:30 on May 20, the 5,443-tonne Saturn V assembly departed the Vehicle Assembly Building atop the crawler-transporter, bound for Launch Pad 39A.

chronology.label: Countdown test commenced
chronology.detail: A countdown test commenced on June 26.

chronology.label: Countdown test concluded
chronology.detail: The countdown test concluded on July 2.

chronology.label: USS Hornet reaches Pearl Harbor
chronology.detail: Hornet reached Pearl Harbor on July 5, embarking recovery teams and media representatives.

chronology.label: USS Hornet departs for recovery area
chronology.detail: With Apollo 11 still on the launch pad, Hornet departed Pearl Harbor for the recovery area in the central Pacific.

chronology.label: Luna 15 launched
chronology.detail: Three days before Apollo 11's launch, the Soviet Union launched Luna 15, which reached lunar orbit before Apollo 11.

chronology.label: Launch complex floodlit and fueling begins
chronology.detail: The launch complex was floodlit on the night of July 15, when the crawler-transporter carried the mobile service structure back to its parking area. In the early hours of the morning, the fuel tanks were filled with liquid hydrogen.

chronology.label: Apollo 11 Launch
chronology.detail: Saturn V AS-506 launched Apollo 11 on July 16, 1969, at 13:32:00 UTC (9:32:00 EDT) from Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A.

chronology.label: S-IC first stage separation
chronology.detail: Full shutdown of the first-stage engines occurred about 2 minutes and 42 seconds into the mission, followed by separation of the S-IC.

chronology.label: S-II separation, S-IVB ignition
chronology.detail: The second stage engines cut off and separated at about 9 minutes and 8 seconds, allowing the first ignition of the S-IVB engine a few seconds later.

chronology.label: Earth orbit insertion
chronology.detail: Apollo 11 entered a near-circular Earth orbit at an altitude of 100.4 nautical miles by 98.9 nautical miles, twelve minutes into its flight.

chronology.label: Trans-lunar injection
chronology.detail: After one and a half orbits, the S-IVB engine was ignited to push the spacecraft onto its trajectory toward the Moon, which took about 5 minutes and 47 seconds.

chronology.label: CSM-LM docking
chronology.detail: Columbia docked with Eagle, which was still attached to the S-IVB stage.

chronology.label: Lunar orbit insertion
chronology.detail: Apollo 11 passed behind the Moon and fired its service propulsion engine to enter lunar orbit.

chronology.label: Armstrong and Aldrin enter Eagle
chronology.detail: At 12:52:00 UTC on July 20, Aldrin and Armstrong entered Eagle and began the final preparations for lunar descent.

chronology.label: Eagle undocking from Columbia
chronology.detail: Eagle separated from Columbia for the descent to the lunar surface.

chronology.label: Lunar landing
chronology.detail: Eagle landed at Tranquility Base in the Sea of Tranquility (Mare Tranquillitatis) with 216 pounds of usable fuel remaining.

chronology.label: Preparations for EVA begin
chronology.detail: Preparations for Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to walk on the Moon began at 23:43 UTC, taking longer than expected at three and a half hours instead of two.

chronology.label: Eagle hatch opened
chronology.detail: Eagle's hatch was opened at 02:39:33 UTC.

chronology.label: Armstrong begins descent to lunar surface
chronology.detail: Armstrong began his descent to the lunar surface at 02:51 UTC.

chronology.label: Armstrong's first step on the Moon
chronology.detail: Six and a half hours after landing, Armstrong stepped off Eagle's landing pad and declared: 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.'

chronology.label: Aldrin joins Armstrong on lunar surface
chronology.detail: Aldrin joined Armstrong on the surface approximately nineteen minutes after Armstrong's first step.

chronology.label: Lunar surface EVA operations
chronology.detail: Armstrong and Aldrin spent around two and a half hours walking on the surface, planting an American flag, speaking with President Richard Nixon, deploying scientific instruments, and collecting 21.5 kg of lunar material.

chronology.label: Lunar module hatch closed
chronology.detail: The hatch was closed again at 05:11:13 UTC after the astronauts transferred the samples and equipment back to the LM.

chronology.label: Eagle ascent stage launch from Moon
chronology.detail: Roughly two hours after awakening, at 17:54:00 UTC, the Apollo 11 crew on the surface safely lifted off in Eagle's ascent stage to rejoin Collins aboard Columbia in lunar orbit.

chronology.label: Eagle rendezvous with Columbia
chronology.detail: Eagle rendezvoused with Columbia at 21:24 UTC on July 21.

chronology.label: Eagle docking with Columbia
chronology.detail: The two spacecraft docked at 21:35 UTC.

chronology.label: Eagle ascent stage jettisoned
chronology.detail: Eagle's ascent stage was jettisoned into lunar orbit at 23:41:31 UTC.

chronology.label: Luna 15 crashes on Moon
chronology.detail: During descent, Luna 15 malfunctioned and crashed in Mare Crisium about two hours before Armstrong and Aldrin took off from the Moon's surface.

chronology.label: Television broadcast from Apollo 11 during return
chronology.detail: On July 23, the last night before splashdown, the three astronauts made a television broadcast in which they reflected on the mission's significance.

chronology.label: Drogue parachutes deployed
chronology.detail: Columbia's drogue parachutes were deployed at 16:44 UTC on July 24.

chronology.label: Splashdown
chronology.detail: Columbia struck the water at 13°19′N 169°9′W, 2,660 km east of Wake Island and 24 km from USS Hornet.

chronology.label: Recovery helicopter lands on USS Hornet
chronology.detail: After touchdown on Hornet at 17:53 UTC, the helicopter was lowered into the hangar bay, where the astronauts walked to the mobile quarantine facility.

chronology.label: USS Hornet returns to Pearl Harbor
chronology.detail: Hornet returned to Pearl Harbor on July 26, welcomed by thousands of people.

chronology.label: Mobile Quarantine Facility airlifted to Houston
chronology.detail: The MQF was airlifted to Houston on July 27, landing on July 27.

chronology.label: Astronauts arrive at Lunar Receiving Laboratory
chronology.detail: The astronauts arrived at the Lunar Receiving Laboratory at 10:00 UTC on July 28.

chronology.label: Columbia arrives at Lunar Receiving Laboratory
chronology.detail: Columbia was flown to Houston in a Douglas C-133 Cargomaster, reaching the Lunar Receiving Laboratory on July 30.

chronology.label: Quarantine lifted
chronology.detail: The Interagency Committee on Back Contamination met in Atlanta and lifted the quarantine on the astronauts and Columbia itself.

chronology.label: Ticker-tape parades
chronology.detail: Apollo 11 crew received ticker-tape parades in New York City and Chicago, with an estimated six million people lining the streets.

chronology.label: Astronauts address Congress
chronology.detail: The astronauts addressed a joint session of Congress, where they presented two American flags that had traveled to the lunar surface.

chronology.label: World goodwill tour begins
chronology.detail: The 38-day world goodwill tour titled 'Giant Leap' began on September 29 and concluded on November 5, 1969, visiting 22 countries.

quotes.text: I believe that this nation should commit itself to achieving the goal, before this decade [1960s] is out, of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to the Earth. No single space project in this period will be more impressive to mankind, or more important for the long-range exploration of space; and none will be so difficult or expensive to accomplish.
quotes.speaker: President John F. Kennedy

quotes.text: We choose to go to the Moon! We choose to go to the Moon ... We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard; because that goal will serve to organize and measure the best of our energies and skills, because that challenge is one that we are willing to accept, one we are unwilling to postpone, and one we intend to win, and the others, too.
quotes.speaker: President John F. Kennedy

quotes.text: This is the LM pilot. I'd like to take this opportunity to ask every person listening in, whoever and wherever they may be, to pause for a moment and contemplate the events of the past few hours and to give thanks in his or her own way.
quotes.speaker: Buzz Aldrin
quotes.src: p55, p1003 (quote from Lunar surface operations section)

quotes.speaker: Neil Armstrong
quotes.context: Lunar descent - after Eagle separates from Columbia

quotes.text: Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.
quotes.speaker: Neil Armstrong

quotes.text: That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
quotes.speaker: Neil Armstrong
quotes.context: Lunar surface operations - first step on the Moon

quotes.speaker: Buzz Aldrin
quotes.context: Lunar surface operations - describing the lunar surface

quotes.text: It's absolutely no trouble to walk around.
quotes.speaker: Neil Armstrong
quotes.context: Lunar surface operations - about moving in lunar gravity

quotes.speaker: Buzz Aldrin
quotes.context: Landing - indicating footpad contact with lunar surface

quotes.text: Of all the jobs I had to do on the Moon the one I wanted to go the smoothest was the flag raising.
quotes.speaker: Buzz Aldrin
quotes.context: Lunar surface operations - planting the American flag

quotes.text: Nixon: Hello, Neil and Buzz. I'm talking to you by telephone from the Oval Room at the White House. And this certainly has to be the most historic telephone call ever made from the White House.
quotes.speaker: President Richard Nixon
quotes.context: Lunar surface operations - Nixon's phone call to the Moon

quotes.text: Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon July 1969, A. D. We came in peace for all mankind.
quotes.context: Landing - inscription on the lunar module ladder plaque

quotes.text: The ascent stage of the LM separated ... I was concentrating on the computers, and Neil was studying the attitude indicator, but I looked up long enough to see the flag fall over.
quotes.speaker: Buzz Aldrin
quotes.context: Lunar ascent - witnessing the American flag topple

quotes.text: To blame the computer for the Apollo 11 problems is like blaming the person who spots a fire and calls the fire department. Actually, the computer was programmed to do more than recognize error conditions. A complete set of recovery programs was incorporated into the software.
quotes.speaker: Margaret Hamilton
quotes.context: Lunar descent - about the 1202 program alarm
quotes.src: p47, quote from Lunar descent section

quotes.text: Roger, Twan—Tranquility, we copy you on the ground. You got a bunch of guys about to turn blue. We're breathing again.
quotes.speaker: Charles Duke (CAPCOM)
quotes.context: Landing - Mission Control's response to landing confirmation

quotes.text: The responsibility for this flight lies first with history and with the giants of science who have preceded this effort; next with the American people, who have, through their will, indicated their desire; next with four administrations and their Congresses, for implementing that will; and then, with the agency and industry teams that built our spacecraft, the Saturn, the Columbia, the Eagle, and the little EMU, the spacesuit and backpack that was our small spacecraft out on the lunar surface.
quotes.speaker: Astronauts Armstrong, Aldrin, and Collins
quotes.context: Return - final mission statement during television broadcast
quotes.src: quote from Return section, p82 context

quotes.text: It was carried out in a technically brilliant way with risks taken ... that would be inconceivable in the risk-averse world of today ... The Apollo programme is arguably the greatest technical achievement of mankind to date ... nothing since Apollo has come close [to] the excitement that was generated by those astronauts—Armstrong, Aldrin and the 10 others who followed them.
quotes.speaker: British scientists
quotes.context: Legacy - Anniversary events reflecting on Apollo 11

quotes.text: A rat done bit my sister Nell. (with Whitey on the moon) Her face and arms began to swell. (and Whitey's on the moon) I can't pay no doctor bill. (but Whitey's on the moon) Ten years from now I'll be paying still. (while Whitey's on the moon)
quotes.speaker: Gil Scott-Heron
quotes.context: Legacy - Cultural significance, poem 'Whitey on the Moon' (1970)
quotes.src: p104, quote from Cultural significance section
